Title: A generic “preserve editorial intent” instruction failed: prompt-level guardrails didn't prevent editorial drift
Description: A small, generic addition to the Narrative user prompt that asked the agent to preserve Synthesis editorial hierarchy did not keep the intended company-level emphasis. Instead, candidate runs consistently demoted Nuëyon’s company identity/audience and elevated orchestration into the central message, while also introducing unsupported audience and validation claims. The experiment concluded the candidate prompt must not be promoted and production was restored.
Audience: Prompt engineers, Narrative/Compose workflow owners, content-product managers, and editorial ops teams who manage prompt-as-code and model-driven pipelines.
Rationale: Teams that manage prompts and model-driven content need concrete, evidence-based lessons about what kinds of prompt changes actually protect editorial intent. This experiment shows that a single, generic editorial-hierarchy rule can be insufficient and even harmful—so readers can learn to treat such guardrails skeptically, design stronger checks, and avoid unsafe promotions.
Evidence: Facts from the report: the candidate prompt added one generic section titled “Preserve Editorial Intent from the Synthesis.” Three candidate runs (only this prompt changed) produced Narrative mean score 4.00/10 vs baseline 6.00/10 and Compose mean 3.33/10 vs baseline 5.67/10. All three candidate Narrative and Compose runs failed the gate that orchestration remain a supporting explanation (criterion C) and introduced unsupported additions (criterion D) in every run. Examples: candidate outputs made orchestration central, added validation/commitment language, and named an audience of founders/product leaders. Decision: Do not promote; production user prompt restored byte-for-byte (rollback SHA matches baseline). Gaps and uncertainty: only three runs per condition, no temperature/seed control, and provider backend alias may vary—so results show a strong signal in this test but are not statistically broad conclusions about all possible changes.
